newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Evacuees under fire in Albania, envoy urges action.
newsitem.headline: Evacuees under fire in Albania, envoy urges action.

text.p: Foreign troops and the terrified evacuees they were trying to rescue came under fire in Albania on Friday as thousands of expatriates scrambled to escape from growing lawlessness sweeping the Balkan state.

With seized guns, ammunition and other weapons in the hands of anyone who could carry them, including children, European envoy Franz Vranitzky said foreign governments had to send military or police forces to Albania to halt the anarchy.

"I think order can only be established with help from abroad," said the former Austrian chancellor, leading a mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in talks with Albanian government and rebel leaders.

Vranitzky met Albania's new Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, Foreign Minister Arjan Starova and army chief of staff General Adem Copani on board the Italian frigate Aliseo in the Adriatic. They told him the they could no longer cope with the rebellion and breakdown of law and order.

"They pointed out that the Albanian crisis is not a civil war. It is chaos and anarchy and they believe they can overcome it if there is support from abroad," Vranitzky told Reuters in Vienna by telephone from the frigate.

The European Union said it was working closely with the OSCE and NATO to coordinate an urgent response to the Albanian crisis. French President Jacques Chirac said in Montevideo he wanted the EU to contribute to any operation to enforce a political settlement there, his spokeswoman said.
While Vranitzky and his 10-member OSCE delegation continued talks with representatives from rebel towns in the south, the United States and European nations rescued foreign nationals by sea and air.
But the United States suspended its evacuation on Friday after two helicopters came under fire, while German troops exchanged fire with gunmen during their own rescue mission.

The Pentagon said an SA7 shoulder-launched missile was fired at a Marine Cobra helicopter and another Cobra came under small arms attack and returned the fire. But all helicopters involved in the operation returned to their ships.

Germany sent five military helicopters from Bosnia to rescue 105 of its nationals and other Europeans, but one Albanian was injured when German troops traded fire with local gunmen who shot at the evacuees and the aircraft.
An Italian military helicopter involved in the airlift was hit by small arms fire over Tirana, but no one was hurt.
In Geneva, the U.N. refugee agency said on Friday it had urged Italy and Greece to allow Albanians fleeing the violence to enter and stay as long as necessary.

At least 500 Albanians have fled to Italy in a ramshackle flotilla of rusting gunboats, fishing vessels and launches in recent days, raising fears of a repeat of the tide of 40,000 Albanians who crossed the Adriatic in 1991 after Stalinist rule crumbled in Europe's poorest state.
In Tirana, political leaders made repeated attempts to calm the virtual anarchy that has broken out in the past 48 hours as looters loosed off bursts of automatic weapons fire.

Officials at a Tirana military hospital in the Albanian capital said four people were killed and 72 injured by stray bullets overnight. Local media said more than 100 people had died since the unrest erupted earlier this month.

Thousands of Albanians began protests in January after losing their meagre savings in pyramid investment scams. Demonstrations across the south led to clashes with police and the ransacking of army and police arsenals, looting and wild shooting by bands of men and youths.
Most deaths have been caused by stray bullets.
With the army and regular police reluctant to intervene against its own people, Albanian government leaders have acknowledged they are powerless to stop the mayhem.
Vranitzky said he would urge the EU and the OSCE to ask their individual member governments to consider the Tirana government's request to send forces as soon as possible.

"I will urge them today, or at the latest tomorrow, to make a decision one way or the other," he said. "I think the OSCE and the EU countries should give it very thorough thought because this seems to be the most urgent answer the Albanians have to get, otherwise chaos and anarchy will continue."
The appeal for foreign help was part of a larger package of measures agreed between the OSCE and the Albanian government.

The Albanian government also backed an OSCE idea to send in teams of monitors to help modernise the Balkan state's financial institutions, advise on drawing up a constitution and strengthen the respect of human rights and democracy.

Other monitors would help Albania's security forces to collect the thousands of arms seized across the country -- one of the most difficult proposals which needs the backing of town committees if it is to have even a slim chance of working.
